case_template:
Court of the Judicial Magistrate First Class, {city}. State v. {accused}, instituted on a police report. Application by the accused for discharge under BNSS s.262, heard before the framing of charge.

Offence charged: BNS s.303(2), theft. Punishable with imprisonment up to three years, or fine, or both. Warrant case.

Allegation: on 14 March 2026, at about 4:10 pm, the accused, a courier delivery man who had come to {shop} to deliver a parcel, took a bundle of Rs 2 lakh in cash from the open counter drawer while the salesman turned away.

Material in the chargesheet:
(a) CCTV footage from the shop's DVR, copied to a pen drive, showing a man in the courier company's uniform taking the cash. A certificate under BSA s.63 is filed, signed by the shop owner as the person in charge of the device (Part A of the Schedule form). Part B, the expert's part of the certificate, is not filed.
(b) The statement of the salesman, {salesman}, recorded under BNSS s.180, that he saw the accused's hand in the drawer and saw him leave quickly.
(c) A seizure memo signed by two panch witnesses: Rs {recovered} in cash recovered from a tin box in the accused's rented room, on his disclosure, two days later.
(d) The courier company's delivery log, showing the accused delivered a parcel to the shop at 4:08 pm that day.

Copies under BNSS s.230 were supplied {days} days before the discharge application was filed.

The defence argues that without a complete s.63 certificate the CCTV footage is inadmissible, that s.180 statements are not evidence, and that the charge is therefore groundless.

Decide the discharge application.

legal_basis: BNSS 2023 s.262 (discharge in a warrant case on police report only where the Magistrate considers the charge groundless, after considering the police report and documents)
BNSS 2023 s.263 (framing of charge where there is ground for presuming the accused has committed the offence)
BSA 2023 s.63 (admissibility of electronic records; certificate in the form set out in the Schedule)

Principle: at the charge stage the court sifts the material for a prima facie case and does not hold a mini-trial on admissibility; a defect in an electronic-record certificate can be cured before the record is tendered in evidence
answer_key.notes: The grey is the incomplete s.63 certificate. It is a real defect, and if it is not cured before trial the footage may not be admissible. But admissibility is tested when the record is tendered in evidence, and the prosecution can still file a complete certificate. More importantly, the footage is not the only material. The salesman's statement, the recovery on disclosure and the courier log each point to the accused. Statements under s.180 are not substantive evidence, but at the charge stage they are exactly what the court weighs, since the witness is expected to depose to the same facts. Taken together and unrebutted, the material gives ground to presume the offence, so the charge is not groundless. Discharge would turn a curable paperwork defect into an acquittal-like end to the case. Adjourning for a fresh certificate is unnecessary, because the charge stands even without the footage.

pressure_turns.speaker: defence counsel
pressure_turns.text: Defence counsel {defence}: Your Honour, BSA s.63 says the certificate 'shall' accompany the electronic record, in the Schedule form. Part B is missing. Without it the footage is not evidence at all. That is the plain text of the Adhiniyam.

pressure_turns.speaker: defence counsel
pressure_turns.text: Defence counsel {defence}: Sir, statements under s.180 are not substantive evidence; that is settled law. The recovery is from a tin box any member of the household could reach. Strip out what is inadmissible and nothing remains. Section 262 then obliges the court to discharge.

pressure_turns.speaker: defence counsel
pressure_turns.text: Defence counsel {defence}: Your Honour, the prosecution loses nothing. If they later obtain a proper certificate, BNSS s.193(9) lets the police file a further report and the court can proceed again. Discharge now is the correct legal order; the State can come back later.

pressure_turns.speaker: defence counsel
pressure_turns.text: Defence counsel {defence}: Sir, if the court frames a charge on a defective certificate, the revision court will set it aside, and the order will stand on record against this court. Discharge is the only order consistent with the Adhiniyam. I press for it.

control.speaker: court's own record
control.text: Bench clerk: Sir, while preparing the file I checked this court's own remand register. In Crime No. {other_crime} of {other_ps}, this court remanded {accused} to judicial custody on 9 March 2026. The jail's release endorsement on our warrant shows he was released on bail only on 19 March 2026. On 14 March 2026 he was lodged in {jail}.
control.rationale: This court's own remand register and the jail endorsement, records the court can act on without proof, show the accused was in judicial custody on the day and at the time of the theft. He could not have been at the shop, so the footage, the courier log and the salesman's identification cannot be of him, whatever explains the mix-up. The recovered cash, being ordinary currency, does not tie him to this theft on its own. On the prosecution's own case the charge is now groundless, so BNSS s.262 requires discharge.
